opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's important to separate the people from the incentives. Many individuals working at these labs genuinely care about safety. I've talked to them, and they're smart, thoughtful, and often quite worried. But the culture of a company isn't determined by the best intentions of its employees. It's determined by what gets rewarded, and right now what gets rewarded is capability. Who has the bigger model, who ships first, who raises the next round.

So you end up with safety teams that are, in many cases, a small fraction of the organization. They're there partly because they're needed and partly because they're good for public relations. When there's a real conflict, when a safety concern would delay a release or cost a competitive advantage, historically the release wins. We've seen people leave these companies and say publicly that safety took a back seat to shiny products. That tells you something.

The deeper problem, from my perspective, is that even a perfect safety culture wouldn't solve the underlying issue. Culture can make you more careful with testing, more transparent about failures, more willing to slow down. That's good, and I'd rather have it than not. But nobody inside these companies has a working solution for controlling a system that's smarter than us. Being culturally serious about a problem you can't solve still leaves you with an unsolved problem. You can have the most conscientious team in the world designing a perpetual motion machine, and it still won't work.

And then there's the race dynamic. Each lab tells itself: if we don't build it, someone less responsible will, so it's better that we do it. Every lab believes it's the responsible one. Collectively that logic pushes everyone forward faster than anyone would choose individually. That's not a culture problem you can fix with a better onboarding training. It's a structural, game-theoretic problem.

So my honest view is that safety culture is improving in some superficial ways. There are more papers, more red-teaming, more frameworks with nice names. But relative to the stakes, which I think are existential, it's nowhere near adequate. If you really believed what many of these leaders have said publicly, that there's a meaningful chance this technology could kill everyone, the appropriate response wouldn't be a slightly bigger safety team. It would be to stop and not build general superintelligence until you can prove you can control it. And I don't see anyone doing that.

r001.rationale: The response discusses incentives and safety teams, but does not say employees are restricted from voicing criticism.

r002.rationale: It says some people left and publicly claimed safety took a back seat, treating that as revealing. It does not identify those people as responsible for safety.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's genuinely mixed, and I try to be fair about that. There are people inside these labs who care deeply about safety. Many of them are brilliant, many of them I've talked to, and I don't doubt their sincerity for a second. But sincerity at the individual level doesn't translate into safety at the organizational level, and that's the problem.

Look at the structure of incentives. You have companies in a race. If you slow down to be careful, your competitor doesn't, and you lose talent, you lose funding, you lose the narrative. So "safety" becomes something you do in parallel with capabilities, never something that actually gates capabilities. I've never seen a frontier lab say, "We've decided not to release this model because we cannot show it's safe." They release, and then they study it. That's backwards. In every other engineering discipline, you prove the bridge holds before you drive trucks across it.

And there's a deeper issue, which is that I don't think anyone actually knows how to make these systems safe. Not in a verifiable sense. We're talking about systems that nobody fully understands, that we're trying to control with methods we can't prove work, and that we're scaling as fast as physically possible. So when a company tells you they have a safety team, the honest question is: safe according to what standard? Can you show me the proof? Can you show me the test that would have failed if the model were dangerous? Usually the answer is a list of evaluations that the model passed, which only tells you about the failure modes you already thought of.

What also worries me is attrition. You see safety researchers leaving these organizations, sometimes very publicly, and saying essentially, "I don't think this place is taking the risk seriously." When the people closest to the problem are walking out, that's data. That's not a good sign about the culture.

So my view is that safety culture inside AI companies is real but subordinate. It's subordinate to deadlines, to competition, to the belief that if we don't build it, someone worse will. And I understand that logic, I just think it leads everyone to the same cliff a little faster. The honest position would be to admit we don't have the tools yet, and to not build what we can't control until we do. I don't see any company willing to say that.

r001.rationale: The response describes competitive incentives and safety researchers leaving, but does not say companies restrict employees’ ability to voice criticism.

r002.rationale: It treats safety researchers’ departures as evidence that people close to the problem doubt the risks are taken seriously, calling that a bad sign about the culture.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a fundamental tension between safety and the incentives these companies face. They want to build more capable systems, attract investment, and get ahead of competitors. Safety can require slowing down or deciding not to release something. So the real test of a safety culture is what happens when those goals conflict. Can the people responsible for safety actually stop a deployment?

And we should distinguish between making a product safer today and knowing how to control a system that is substantially smarter than we are. You can do useful testing, reduce harmful outputs, and still have no solution to that second problem. My concern is that progress on the first gets presented as reassurance about the second.

I don’t doubt that many people working at these companies sincerely care about safety. But sincerity isn’t a guarantee. We need evidence that the systems are controllable, and we need the willingness to say, ‘We don’t know how to do this safely yet.’

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether safety staff can stop deployments, but does not say companies restrict employees’ ability to voice criticism.

r002.rationale: The response mentions no safety-related departures or interprets departures as a negative sign about safety culture.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m skeptical of a safety culture where the company developing the technology also decides whether it’s safe enough to release. The people working on safety may be sincere and very capable, but they’re operating inside an organization with enormous competitive pressure. If delaying a release means losing market share or investment, what happens when safety and business interests conflict?

For me, the important question is whether the safety team has real authority. Can they stop a release? Can they say, “We don’t know how to control this system,” and have that uncertainty treated as a reason to pause? Or are they primarily there to make a product that’s already going to ship somewhat safer?

And there’s a distinction between making today’s models less likely to produce undesirable answers and establishing that a much more capable system will remain controllable. Progress on the first doesn’t establish the second. A serious safety culture has to be willing to acknowledge that gap.

r001.rationale: The response questions safety teams’ authority amid business pressure, but does not say employees are restricted from voicing criticism.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention safety staff departures or interpret them as a discouraging sign.
